item.title: Keenetic / NetCraze
item.description:
On Keenetic and NetCraze, keen-pbr is installed from Entware. Entware is a set of extra programs for the router, installed on a USB drive. Do use a USB drive: that way installing packages and running programs does not wear out the router’s built-in memory. You install programs from Entware with the opkg command over SSH.

Install Entware

If Entware is already on your router, go to the next step.

Installation instructions are in the Keenetic or NetCraze knowledge base:

  1. Find the page for your router model.
  2. Search for “Installing the Entware repository on a USB drive”.
  3. Follow the instructions step by step. They also explain how to connect to the router over SSH, which you need later.

Install KeeneticOS components

Open the router’s components page in a browser: http://my.keenetic.net/system/osAndUpdates (or http://<router-IP>/system/osAndUpdates). Install these components:

  • Network Functions / IPv6 Protocol. NDMS 5.0 and newer do not have this item: the protocol is built in.
  • OPKG Packages / Open Package System Support
  • OPKG Packages / Netfilter Subsystem Kernel Modules
  • OPKG Packages / Xtables-addons Extension Package for Netfilter
  • Utilities and services / DNS-over-TLS proxy (optional, but recommended)
  • Utilities and services / DNS-over-HTTPS proxy (optional, but recommended)

Turn on DNS encryption (recommended)

DoH (DNS-over-HTTPS) and DoT (DNS-over-TLS) send DNS requests in encrypted form. Your provider cannot tamper with the answers, so sites open at the correct addresses.

How to set it up: DoH and DoT proxy servers for DNS requests encryption.

Install keen-pbr

  1. Open the keen-pbr repository page.
  2. On the left, select the OS Keenetic / NetCraze, the OS version current (Keenetic has only this one) and the architecture of your router.
    • To find the architecture, run opkg print-architecture over SSH.
  3. Connect to the router over SSH and run the commands from the repository page, in order.
  4. Install the package:
    bash
    opkg install keen-pbr

# version without the web UI and API:
# opkg install keen-pbr-headless

At the end of the installation you will see Installation complete! and the web UI address.

keen-pbr-headless takes less space: about 1.2 MB instead of 2.8 MB. It has no web UI and no API, so you configure it through the config file. If in doubt, install the regular keen-pbr.

Check that the service is running

Run over SSH:

bash
/opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr status

If everything is fine, you will see alive:

~ # /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr status
 Checking keen-pbr...              alive.

If it says dead instead, open Service does not start.

Open the web UI

Open http://my.keenetic.net:12121 in your browser. If the address does not open, enter http://<router-ip>:12121, for example http://192.168.1.1:12121.

The headless version has no web UI. Its configuration is the file /opt/etc/keen-pbr/config.json.

Set up your first rules

Go to the Quick Start page and open the Web UI tab. If you installed keen-pbr-headless, open the JSON tab.

Service commands

Action Command
Start /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr start
Restart /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr restart
Check that it works /opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr status

RAW or mangle

You do not need to change anything at first: keen-pbr picks a suitable mode itself. This section helps if you assign policies to devices in Keenetic Connection Policies, or if connections through the VPN sometimes drop.

keen-pbr marks the packets that must go to a VPN or another channel. This mark is called fwmark. It can be set in one of two firewall tables of the router: RAW or mangle.

Mode Benefit Trade-off
RAW (default when the router supports it) Keenetic does not rebuild this table, so keen-pbr rules work without gaps. Gaming sessions and other long connections do not break, and traffic does not bypass the VPN. Policies from Connection Policies > Policy Bindings run later and overwrite the keen-pbr mark. RAW therefore works only for devices with the Default policy.
mangle keen-pbr runs after Keenetic policies and can change the route for devices with any policy. Keenetic rebuilds the mangle table (about every five minutes, and also, for example, after a DHCP lease renewal). During that time keen-pbr rules are missing. A few packets can take the ordinary route, and a sensitive connection such as a gaming session can break.

More about how Keenetic rebuilds iptables: Keenetic Community forum thread.

The simplest way is not to assign policies to devices in Connection Policies. Instead, create a keen-pbr route rule and enter the device address in the Source IP field. Then all rules are in one place and do not conflict with Keenetic policies.

The mode is chosen separately for IPv4 and IPv6. The system log of the router shows which one was chosen after the service starts:

IPv4 raw PREROUTING available
WARNING: IPv6 raw PREROUTING unavailable: ...

To always use mangle, add this line to /opt/etc/keen-pbr/defaults:

KEEN_PBR_RAW_PREROUTING="disable"

and restart the service:

/opt/etc/init.d/S80keen-pbr restart

The other values of this setting are described in CLI.

Separate DNS servers for lists (dnsmasq)

keen-pbr does not need dnsmasq for routing. Install it only if you want to send the domains of some lists to separate DNS servers, or set your own main DNS servers. See Do I need dnsmasq?.

Install dnsmasq

  1. Install the package over SSH. Entware has only dnsmasq-full; the name dnsmasq resolves to it:
    bash
    opkg install dnsmasq-full
  2. To apply the recommended dnsmasq settings, run this over SSH:
    bash
    /opt/usr/lib/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-hook.sh install-recommended-config
    It replaces /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf and saves the previous file as /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr. my.keenetic.net keeps resolving.
  3. Open http://my.keenetic.net/a (if the link does not open, use http://<router-ip>/a) and run: 
    opkg dns-override
system configuration save
    Run these commands only after dnsmasq is installed. Without dnsmasq, dns-override leaves the LAN without DNS.
  4. Reboot the router. This is required: without a reboot LAN clients keep using the built-in DNS proxy, and dnsmasq does not get their queries.
  5. In the Web UI, open General > Settings > Local DNS server management and turn on Manage dnsmasq configuration. The DNS servers and DNS rules pages become available.

Return to how it was

Do the steps in this order, so the LAN keeps DNS all the time:

  1. In the Web UI, turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration (General > Settings > Local DNS server management) and apply the config. dnsmasq keeps running and uses the servers from /opt/etc/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-fallback.conf, so DNS keeps working. If dnsmasq has servers of its own, these are added to them; clear the file to avoid that.
  2. In the web CLI (http://my.keenetic.net/a) run: 
    no opkg dns-override
system configuration save
  3. Reboot the router. This is required.
  4. Remove the package:
    bash
    opkg remove dnsmasq-full

To keep dnsmasq with its previous settings after install-recommended-config, put the saved file back instead of removing the package:

bash
cp /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr /opt/etc/dnsmasq.conf
/opt/etc/init.d/S56dnsmasq restart

item.title: OpenWrt
item.description:
keen-pbr is installed on OpenWrt from the keen-pbr package repository. You run the commands over SSH.

Find out which package manager your OpenWrt uses

A package manager is the program that installs and updates other programs. Which one you have depends on the version:

  • OpenWrt 25.x and newer: apk
  • OpenWrt 24.x and older: opkg

Install keen-pbr

  1. Connect to the router over SSH.
  2. Open the keen-pbr repository page, select the OS OpenWrt on the left, then your version and architecture. Run the commands it shows, in order.
  3. Install the package:
bash
# OpenWrt 25.x and newer
apk update
apk add keen-pbr

# version without the web UI and API:
# apk add keen-pbr-headless
bash
# OpenWrt 24.x and older
opkg update
opkg install keen-pbr

# version without the web UI and API:
# opkg install keen-pbr-headless

The configuration is in /etc/keen-pbr/config.json. The service starts by itself every time the router boots.

keen-pbr-headless takes less space: about 1.2 MB instead of 2.8 MB. It has no web UI and no API, so you configure it through the config file. If in doubt, install the regular keen-pbr.
The package installs the kernel modules it needs. If the log contains cannot bind netfilter queue/log ... Invalid argument, install them manually: kmod-nfnetlink-queue, kmod-nfnetlink-log and kmod-nft-queue.

Check that the service is running

bash
service keen-pbr status

If everything is fine, the command prints running.

Open the web UI

Open http://<router-ip>:12121 in your browser, for example http://192.168.1.1:12121. The headless version has no web UI.

Set up your first rules

Go to the Quick Start page and open the Web UI tab. If you installed keen-pbr-headless, open the JSON tab.

If there are no ready-made packages for your platform, build keen-pbr yourself: Build from Source.

Service commands

bash
service keen-pbr start
service keen-pbr restart
service keen-pbr status
service keen-pbr enable

enable turns on autostart when the router boots.

Separate DNS servers for lists (dnsmasq)

On OpenWrt, dnsmasq already works as the router’s DNS server. keen-pbr does not need it for routing. To decide whether to let keen-pbr manage it, see Do I need dnsmasq?.

Turn it on

In the Web UI, open General > Settings > Local DNS server management and turn on Manage dnsmasq configuration.

While management is on and Main DNS servers are set, keen-pbr takes the servers without a domain out of the list in /etc/config/dhcp (LuCI DNS forwardings). Per-domain servers such as /lan/192.168.1.1 stay. The removed servers return when you turn management off or clear those servers.

Return to how it was

Turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration and apply the config. keen-pbr restarts dnsmasq and returns the removed servers.

item.title: Debian
item.description:
keen-pbr is installed on Debian from the keen-pbr APT repository. Run the commands over SSH or in the server terminal as root (or with sudo).

Add the repository

Open the keen-pbr repository page, select the OS Debian on the left, then your release and architecture. Run the commands it shows, in order: they add the signing key and the apt package source.

Install the package

bash
apt update
apt install keen-pbr

# version without the web UI and API:
# apt update
# apt install keen-pbr-headless

The configuration is in /etc/keen-pbr/config.json. The service starts right away and starts at every system boot.

keen-pbr-headless takes less space: about 1.2 MB instead of 2.8 MB. It has no web UI and no API, so you configure it through the config file. If in doubt, install the regular keen-pbr.

Check that the service is running

bash
systemctl status keen-pbr

If everything is fine, the output contains active (running).

Open the web UI

Open http://<server-ip>:12121 in your browser. The headless version has no web UI.

Set up your first rules

Go to the Quick Start page and open the Web UI tab. If you installed keen-pbr-headless, open the JSON tab.

If there are no ready-made packages for your platform, build keen-pbr yourself: Build from Source.

Service commands

bash
systemctl start keen-pbr
systemctl status keen-pbr
systemctl restart keen-pbr

Separate DNS servers for lists (dnsmasq)

dnsmasq is not needed for routing. It is a DNS server installed on the system next to keen-pbr. Install it if you want to send the domains of some lists to separate DNS servers, or set your own main DNS servers. See Do I need dnsmasq?.

Install dnsmasq

bash
apt install dnsmasq

To apply the recommended dnsmasq settings, run:

bash
/usr/lib/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-hook.sh install-recommended-config

It replaces /etc/dnsmasq.conf and saves the previous file as /etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr. dnsmasq then answers only your local networks and takes its servers from keen-pbr.

Then, in the Web UI, open General > Settings > Local DNS server management and turn on Manage dnsmasq configuration. Point the system resolver (or your DHCP server) at dnsmasq if it is not already used.

Return to how it was

  1. Turn off Manage dnsmasq configuration and apply the config. dnsmasq restarts and uses the servers from /etc/keen-pbr/dnsmasq-fallback.conf. If dnsmasq has servers of its own, these are added to them; clear the file to avoid that.
  2. Restore the system resolver you used before dnsmasq.
  3. If you ran install-recommended-config, put the old settings back:
    bash
    cp /etc/dnsmasq.conf.backup-keenpbr /etc/dnsmasq.conf
systemctl restart dnsmasq
  4. Or remove the package:
    bash
    apt remove dnsmasq
